1.pericope_label: And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber’s razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair. Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them. Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts. Then take of them again, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire; for thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott would render the order take thee a sharp sword and use it as a barber's razor, noting that the same word recurs in the next verse translated both ways, finds the nearer allusion in the older prophet's picture of judgment as a shaving with a hired razor, observes that a priest was forbidden by the law to shave head or beard so that a priest shorn with a sword announced a desolation of the first order, insists the weighing proves the certainty of the judgment rather than making the scene vivid, thinks the burning was described rather than performed, and marks the point where symbol gives way to the parallelisms of Hebrew verse.

Gill allows the word its general sense of anything that cuts asunder and identifies the handful in the skirts with the vinedressers left behind by the captain of the guard and those who came back from Egypt; Calvin wants a true balance so that no portion outweighs another, presses hair as the image of a multitude past counting which was the city's own boast and bred the confidence that destroyed it, concludes that since not a hair is left not a man escapes, and sees the covenant at stake in the handful, a seed kept back or the nation would have gone the way of Sodom, though some even of that handful burn.

Clarke reaches the same result about the instrument from the period's toolkit, where edge-tools were few and the sword served as knife and razor by turns, and sets out the whole allegory in order, the prophet the nation, his hair the people, the razor the invader, the division the kinds of punishment, with burning for famine and plague, the stroke about the walls for those killed in sorties and storming, and the scattered portion for the deported; Wesley compresses the shaving into mourning, reproach and deformity, and names quarrels and conspiracies as the causes of the second fire.

Henry makes the man himself the sign and reads his willingness as evidence that he did not want the day he foretold, develops the hair as a burden its owner wishes rid of so that the whole growth and not the superfluous part must go, gathers the associations of ignominy, mourning and the ended Nazarite vow, takes the balances for a justice that weighs men and actions without error, and concludes that those will be ruined who will not be reformed.

positions.position: A sharp sword, taken for its symbolism and used as a razor; the same word is rendered both ways in the next verse.
One implement only, since edge-tools were few and the sword served as knife and razor by turns.
The word means any sharp thing by which something is cut asunder.

outliers.claim: Grounds the force of the sign in the shorn man's priesthood, since the law forbade a priest to shave head or beard, so that a priest shaved with a sword was itself the announcement of desolation.
Reads the shaving as the end of the city's Nazarite standing as well as its honour, since shaving closed that vow and the place could no longer be called holy.

themes: And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber’s razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair.

Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them.
Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts.
Then take of them again, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire; for thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel.

5.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her. And she hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations, and my statutes more than the countries that are round about her: for they have refused my judgments and my statutes, they have not walked in them.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch head these verses as the divine word that explains the symbols by giving the cause of the judgment, with the execution beginning further on; Ellicott turns the central position into a map and an argument, listing the neighbours on every side and the trade reaching to India, arguing that a people so placed could have become the missionary of monotheism while deserts, sea and mountains still let them develop undisturbed, showing how the same position made them prey once the bond of unity weakened, concluding that responsibility is proportioned to privilege, and preferring wickedly resisted to changed while denying that the Israelites were actually worse in conduct than the heathen.

Gill lets the identification cover both signs, the drawing on the tile and the shorn head, calls the place chief not merely of its own country, and reports that the disputed verb may mean rebelled against or transgressed although the older Jewish authorities keep changed; Calvin insists the praise is not praise but a recital of benefits meant to reprove, since contempt of gifts is sacrilege and visibility completes the disgrace, refuses as puerile the fancy that the phrase claims the earth's exact centre, takes the sense to be the most celebrated part of the world, hears the demonstrative as emphatic and the city as the most beautiful part of a theatre, and locates the aggravation in knowledge rather than in comparative wickedness.

Clarke entertains the geographical claim, allows it roughly defensible, then observes that the true land centre of a hemisphere falls on the capital of his own empire, and holds plainly that the Jews were worse than their neighbours, since idolatrous nations kept more morality than they did and men who fall from a height become more abominable in proportion to it, which he calls the common case of backsliders.

Henry treats the naming of the sign as ordinary scriptural usage, the thing signified lending its name to the sign, takes the shaved head for a city stripped and emptied, denies that the place stood in a remote corner, and presses two senses of its central position, a hill raised above hills and watched by all in goodwill or malice, and a candle set on a stand to carry light outward until the design finally waited for the day the word went out into all nations.

debates.question: Were the Israelites actually worse than the surrounding heathen?

positions.position: Yes: idolatrous as the neighbours were, they kept more morality, and men who fall from a height become more abominable in proportion to it.
No: the Israelites were in fact far better, and the sentence is relative to the light given rather than absolute.
The aggravation lies in knowledge, a yoke shaken off knowingly with no excuse left once instruction has come from the divine mouth.

debates.question: What does the phrase about being set in the midst claim?

positions.position: Not the earth's exact centre, which is a puerile fancy, but the most celebrated part of the world.
The geographical claim is roughly defensible, though the true land centre of a hemisphere lies elsewhere.
A position among the chief kingdoms of antiquity, which was both the great opportunity and the chief source of disaster.

outliers.claim: Turns the question of the world's centre into a claim about his own day, that the point centring the greatest landmass of a hemisphere is the capital of the British empire.
Reads the magnificent praise of the city as calculated disgrace, the place set on a platform so that its dignity shows from every side and its ingratitude with it.

themes: Thus saith the Lord God; This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her.

And she hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations, and my statutes more than the countries that are round about her: for they have refused my judgments and my statutes, they have not walked in them.

7.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Because ye multiplied more than the nations that are round about you, and have not walked in my statutes, neither have kept my judgments, neither have done according to the judgments of the nations that are round about you; Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I, even I, am against thee, and will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the nations. And I will do in thee that which I have not done, and whereunto I will not do any more the like, because of all thine abominations.

schools.summary: Ellicott would render the disputed verb raged rather than multiplied, the sense it carries in the psalm about the nations and the one the lexicons give, sets out both readings of the clause about the judgments of the nations and prefers the one that makes Israel fail to keep revealed law as faithfully as the heathen kept what nature taught them, ties the publicity of the sentence to the conspicuousness of the city, and rejects any reading that makes the unexampled judgment a comparison between one calamity on this people and another rather than between God's dealings with them and with everyone else.

Gill notes that the sins having been set out the sentence now follows, hears in the doubled pronoun an omnipotent king declaring himself an adversary, and lists what the unexampled judgment must outdo: the flood, the fire on Sodom, the plagues in Egypt, the expulsion of the Canaanites; Calvin canvasses three readings of the disputed verb and rejects two as forced and far-fetched before settling for increase, twice refuses the older interpretation that excludes angels and human agents or softens the executing of judgments into a promise of moderation, explains that common punishments are despised so the ordinary measure had to be exceeded, and declines to read the coming horror as metaphor.

Clarke reads the unexampled judgment as a comparison of catastrophes and names two, the sack under Nebuchadnezzar and the worse one under Titus, calling them unparalleled in human history; Wesley takes the increase to be in idols and superstitions rather than in people, holds without hesitation that they exceeded the heathen in superstition and fell short of them in moral virtue, and finds the difference from flood and fire in duration, since those killed quickly and this would not.

debates.question: What does the clause about the judgments of the nations mean?

positions.position: That Israel failed to keep revealed law as faithfully as the heathen kept what nature and tradition taught them; behaving exactly as they did would already be deeper unfaithfulness.
That they exceeded the heathen in superstition and idolatry and fell short of them in the moral virtues.

debates.question: What is the unexampled judgment compared with?

positions.position: Other catastrophes on the same people: the sack under Nebuchadnezzar and the worse one under Titus, unparalleled in history.
Not other judgments on this people at all, but God's dealings with them against his dealings with every other nation.
The ordinary measure of chastisement, which had to be exceeded because common punishments are despised.
The flood, the fire on Sodom, the plagues in Egypt and the expulsion of the Canaanites, none of which it will resemble.

outliers.claim: Refuses the reading that makes the doubled pronoun exclude angels and human agents, since the Assyrians and Chaldeans were plainly used as scourges, and denies that executing judgments asserts a measured or lenient punishment: it means only exercising jurisdiction.
Finds the difference between this judgment and the flood or the fire on Sodom in duration rather than severity, those deaths being quick and this one lingering.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Because ye multiplied more than the nations that are round about you, and have not walked in my statutes, neither have kept my judgments, neither have done according to the judgments of the nations that are round about you;
Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I, even I, am against thee, and will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the nations.
And I will do in thee that which I have not done, and whereunto I will not do any more the like, because of all thine abominations.

10.pericope_label: Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds. Wherefore, as I live, saith the Lord God; Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity. A third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee: and a third part shall fall by the sword round about thee; and I will scatter a third part into all the winds, and I will draw out a sword after them. Thus shall mine anger be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken it in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury in them. Moreover I will make thee waste, and a reproach among the nations that are round about thee, in the sight of all that pass by. So it shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations that are round about thee, when I shall execute judgments in thee in anger and in fury and in furious rebukes. I the Lord have spoken it. When I shall send upon them the evil arrows of famine, which shall be for their destruction, and which I will send to destroy you: and I will increase the famine upon you, and will break your staff of bread: So will I send upon you famine and evil beasts, and they shall bereave thee; and pestilence and blood shall pass through thee; and I will bring the sword upon thee. I the Lord have spoken it.

schools.summary: Ellicott insists on the symmetry of the clauses, nothing inflicted that was not called down, corrects the rendering diminish since its pronoun has nothing behind it and the verb means to withdraw, so that what is withdrawn is presence and compassion, and distinguishes the two senses of the word for comfort, either relenting or consoling oneself by vengeance, judging the second intended so that wounded honour is publicly vindicated.

Gill traces the cannibalism to the law's threat and three sieges and argues that fathers must have shared what is recorded of mothers, notes that the oath is the form which makes revocation impossible, matches the burning third to those consumed by plague and hunger, hears completion in the accomplished anger after a threat long deferred, and offers three ways to take the arrows of famine; Calvin works from the same lament, observes that a surviving name of the people would have been ground for hope and that this is what is refused, points out that the resolution omits the fourth portion hidden in the fold of the garment, rejects the interpreters who took the comforting for a promise of pardon, prefers the sense of drought in the word for waste, and makes the archer image deliberate rather than ornamental, chosen to pierce minds like stone.

Clarke refuses to doubt the cannibalism given the extremities, reads the scattering as deportation among all nations, adds that the displeasure is not transient but settled, recalls that the ancients drew famine and plague as poisoned shafts, and holds that wild animals multiply where a country is emptied while allowing that the invader, often likened to a lion, may be meant; Wesley finds the scattering verified twice, reduces the reason for vengeance to the temple and its idols, glosses the comforting as vengeance executed in zeal for the divine glory, turns the taunt into a proverb, and looks past the nearer ruin to a final one.

debates.question: Is the clause about the anger being accomplished a threat or a mitigation?

positions.position: A threat throughout; the interpreters who read an interposed promise of pardon are refuted by what follows.
A threat: the word means consoling oneself by taking vengeance, not relenting, and wounded honour is vindicated publicly.
Vengeance executed in zeal for the divine glory.
Literally lions, wolves and bears, threatened in the law for disobedience.
Wild animals that multiply wherever a country is emptied, though the invader himself, often likened to a lion, may also be meant.

outliers.claim: Notes that the plain restatement of the sign drops its fourth member, the handful hidden in the fold of the garment, though it was not spoken in vain, God varying his manner of speaking by his own right.
Argues from his own country that wild beasts multiply in depopulated lands, wolves having abounded in England when it was thinly peopled and none remaining once it filled.

themes: Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds.

Wherefore, as I live, saith the Lord God; Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity.

A third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee: and a third part shall fall by the sword round about thee; and I will scatter a third part into all the winds, and I will draw out a sword after them.

Thus shall mine anger be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken it in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury in them.
Moreover I will make thee waste, and a reproach among the nations that are round about thee, in the sight of all that pass by.

So it shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations that are round about thee, when I shall execute judgments in thee in anger and in fury and in furious rebukes. I the Lord have spoken it.

When I shall send upon them the evil arrows of famine, which shall be for their destruction, and which I will send to destroy you: and I will increase the famine upon you, and will break your staff of bread:
So will I send upon you famine and evil beasts, and they shall bereave thee; and pestilence and blood shall pass through thee; and I will bring the sword upon thee. I the Lord have spoken it.
